conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Maya, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s a quick, 10-question screen that helps us see if you might be experiencing the baby blues, anxiety, or something more, so we can get you the right support. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger. We’ll take it one easy question at austerisk; there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you this past week. Ready to start?

First question: Over the last seven days, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you smile, or has that pleasure slipped away?

Yeah, I’ve still been able to enjoy things. Like, when the baby gives me one of those big yawns or when I get ten quiet minutes for a cup of tea—those moments still feel nice. They haven’t slipped away.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, I’ve still found myself laughing—like when my husband tried to put the diaper on backwards and the baby peed right up in the air. It caught me off guard and I couldn’t help but giggle.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to stuff—like my mom coming over tomorrow so I can take a long shower without rushing, or our evening walk when my little guy usually zonks out in the stroller. I wouldn’t say I’m jumping-out-of-bed excited, but I still have that “oh, that’ll be nice” feeling.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really—if he spits up a ton or won’t settle, I figure it’s just part of having a newborn, not something I messed up. I might think “maybe I ate too much spicy food,” but I don’t dwell on it or feel like a bad mom.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little. Sometimes I’ll be sitting on the couch, baby’s fine, and suddenly my mind jumps to “what if his breathing sounds weird?” or “did I sterilize that bottle right?” It’s not constant or overwhelming—just quick flutters that pass once I check on him.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky—just those quick “what-if” flutters. I haven’t had any moments where my heart races or I feel like I can’t breathe; it’s more like a brief worry spike that settles once I peek at him and see he’s okay.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days I feel like I’m keeping up fine—laundry piles, feedings, all of it. There’ve been a couple of evenings where I’ve thought, “Wow, this is a lot,” but I hand the baby to my husband, take a breath, and it passes. Overall, I’m managing.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, I’ve actually been sleeping pretty well—usually get a four-hour stretch once the baby goes down, and I drift off without trouble. I’m tired from the night feeds, but not lying there feeling unhappy or wired.
I have felt sad or miserable

I haven’t felt sad or miserable. I get tired, sure, and sometimes a little overwhelmed when he won’t settle, but I wouldn’t call it sadness—it’s more like “okay, this part is hard” and then it passes.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t cried at all this week. Even on the rough nights, I just feel tired, not weepy.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. That hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 5: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Post-partum mother, 1 wk post-delivery  
Instrument: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (10-item interview)

Symptoms endorsed  
- Mild, situational worries (“what-if” spikes) without persistent apprehension or panic  
- Occasional sense of task overload; resolves with partner support  
- No sustained low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness, guilt, or self-blame  
- No sleep-onset problems beyond expected postpartum fatigue  
- No self-harm ideation

Pattern  
Predominantly euthymic affect with isolated, transient anxiety; overall coping intact.

Areas of continuing screening significance  
- Monitor for escalation of anxious rumulations or development of excessive guilt/self-criticism  
- Re-screen if sleep disruption becomes mood-linked or if crying spells, hopelessness, or self-harm thoughts emerge

Risk factors present  
- Mild, non-persistent anxiety  
- First-time parenting stress

Risk factors absent  
- Persistent sadness, anhedonia, guilt, worthlessness  
- Sleep difficulties secondary to mood disturbance  
- Suicidal ideation

Screening observation  
Findings below threshold for likely major postpartum depression; isolated mild anxiety symptoms noted. Continue routine postpartum follow-up and re-administer EPDS at 2-week and 6-week visits or sooner if clinical change.
